extracted.intended_audience: Citizens and readers weighing the merits of a stronger national government (readers of The Federalist / ratification debates)
extracted.subtask_description: Persuasive political-essay advice and arguments explaining why a single, energetic national government is preferable to multiple independent states or confederacies, with attention to defense, commerce, diplomacy, and internal disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety depends on government, arms, and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The safety of a people 'will tend to repress and discourage' war and 'necessarily depends on the government, the arms, and the resources of the country.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use centralized government capacity, sufficient arms, and national resources to create the best possible state of defense; without effective government these elements cannot be provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: One government can better collect talent and apply uniform policy
rubrics_metrics.description: ''One government can collect and avail itself of the talents and experience of the ablest men... It can move on uniform principles of policy. It can harmonize, assimilate, and protect the several parts and members, and extend the benefit of its foresight and precautions to each.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single national authority is preferred because it can draw on abilities across the whole country and implement coherent policies; examples contrast national advantages with disunited state-by-state action.

rubrics_metrics.name: National government for treaty-making that represents whole
rubrics_metrics.description: ''In the formation of treaties, it will regard the interest of the whole, and the particular interests of the parts as connected with that of the whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treaties negotiated by a central government better balance national and local concerns and avoid conflicting bilateral treaties by separate states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to apply whole resources to defend particular parts
rubrics_metrics.description: ''It can apply the resources and power of the whole to the defense of any particular part, and that more easily and expeditiously than State governments or separate confederacies can possibly do...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralized mobilization enables faster, more effective defense of threatened regions than fragmented state responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia consolidated under one disciplined national plan
rubrics_metrics.description: ''It can place the militia under one plan of discipline, and, by putting their officers in a proper line of subordination to the Chief Magistrate, will, as it were, consolidate them into one corps...''
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize militias under a unified discipline and clear chain of command to make them more efficient than separate state forces; avoid divided, uncoordinated companies.

rubrics_metrics.name: National regulation of navigation fosters naval power
rubrics_metrics.description: ''If one national government had not so regulated the navigation of Britain as to make it a nursery for seamen... their prowess and their thunder would never have been celebrated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A central authority that regulates commerce and navigation can cultivate seamanship and material resources necessary for fleets; multiple governments would dilute that capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union deters foreign provocation; disunion invites interference
rubrics_metrics.description: ''But whatever may be our situation... foreign nations will know and view it exactly as it is; and they will act toward us accordingly... If they see that our national government is efficient... they will be much more disposed to cultivate our friendship than provoke our resentment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign powers judge and react to the observable strength and unity of a polity; a consolidated national government reduces the likelihood of being provoked or exploited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division into multiple sovereignties creates rivalry, jealousy, and danger
rubrics_metrics.description: ''Leave America divided into thirteen... what armies could they raise and pay?... Would there be no danger of their being... flattered into neutrality... or seduced by a too great fondness for peace...?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate confederacies tend toward mutual suspicion, neutrality, or opportunistic behavior; historical examples (Greek city-states, British constituent parts) illustrate risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unequal growth among confederacies produces envy and hostility
rubrics_metrics.description: ''The most sanguine advocates for three or four confederacies cannot reasonably suppose that they would long remain exactly on an equal footing... Whenever... any one... should rise... that moment would those neighbors behold her with envy and with fear.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect differential development to create imbalance and incentives for weaker neighbors to check or undermine a stronger polity, increasing conflict risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different commercial interests lead to divergent foreign alignments
rubrics_metrics.description: ''Each of them would have its commerce with foreigners to regulate by distinct treaties... Different commercial concerns must create different interests, and of course different degrees of political attachment to and connection with different foreign nations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate sovereignties will pursue distinct trade policies and alliances that may pit them against each other; central government avoids contradictory foreign alignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neighboring states tend to be enemies unless constitution prevents it
rubrics_metrics.description: ''NEIGHBORING NATIONS... are naturally enemies of each other unless their common weakness forces them to league in a CONFEDERATE REPUBLIC, and their constitution prevents the differences that neighborhood occasions...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proximity creates rivalry; a confederate constitution or union can extinguish secret jealousy and provide institutional remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of war: ambition, jealousy, commerce, and private passions
rubrics_metrics.description: ''There are some which have a general and almost constant operation... the love of power or the desire of pre-eminence and dominion--the jealousy of power... There are others... the rivalships and competitions of commerce... and there are others... which take their origin entirely in private passions...''
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize multiple human and structural drivers of interstate conflict—policy design must account for ambition, commercial rivalry, and individual actors' private motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial disputes require a common umpire to avoid war
rubrics_metrics.description: ''Territorial disputes have at all times been found one of the most fertile sources of hostility among nations... In the wide field of Western territory, therefore, we perceive an ample theatre for hostile pretensions, without any umpire or common judge to interpose...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide federal mechanisms or courts to adjudicate territorial claims (e.g., western lands) to prevent resort to force; past disputes (Connecticut vs. Pennsylvania; Vermont) illustrate dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competing state commercial policies produce grievances and reprisals
rubrics_metrics.description: ''Each State... would pursue a system of commercial policy peculiar to itself. This would occasion distinctions, preferences, and exclusions, which would beget discontent... The infractions of these regulations... would naturally lead to outrages, and these to reprisals and wars.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform commercial policy or federal oversight reduces incentives for protectionist measures and retaliatory actions between neighboring polities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public debt apportionment is a major potential source of collision
rubrics_metrics.description: ''The public debt of the Union would be a further cause of collision between the separate States or confederacies. The apportionment... would be alike productive of ill-humor and animosity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt clear, equitable rules for apportioning and discharging public debt at the national level; without consensus, disputes over burden-sharing will create deep animosities and defaults.
